q: Does the ~10x CNOT-reduction headline hold when we independently replicate MoG-VQE on BeH2 (8q, paper reports 70 HEA -> 9 MoG-VQE) and LiH (12q, paper reports 12 MoG-VQE) with our reimplementation rather than only on H2 (where our reduction bounds out at ~2x)?
basis: This replication tested only H2/4q/STO-3G. The paper's 10x headline is stated on the larger molecules where the HEA baseline itself needs 60-70+ CNOTs. On H2 the HEA baseline is 6 CNOTs so the maximum possible reduction factor is small. The claim we tested is 'sign and mechanism', not '10x magnitude'.
next_steps: 1) Extend code/mog_vqe_h2.py to accept a molecule spec (geometry, active space, basis). 2) Build BeH2 (linear, 4-electron active, 6 orbitals) and LiH (STO-3G, frozen 1s Li, 6 orbitals) Hamiltonians via pennylane.qchem.molecular_hamiltonian. 3) Increase population to 32-64, generations to 25-50, max NCNOTs to 30-80. 4) Compare to the paper's Fig.3/4/5 Pareto fronts point-by-point. 5) Runtime: ~4-8 h on uicgpu single A100 or ~12-24 h on m1 CPU; both are within budget.

q: Does replacing our COBYLA/L-BFGS-B inner optimizer with an actual CMA-ES (the paper's inner loop) change the achievable-corner picture on larger molecules with higher-dimensional angle spaces (e.g. LiH with ~60 angles at 12 CNOTs), or is inner-loop choice fungible in this regime?
basis: We deliberately substituted COBYLA / L-BFGS-B multistart as a same-class stand-in. On H2 this is fine (both hit machine precision at 3 CNOTs). But CMA-ES's covariance-matrix adaptation is specifically designed for higher-D noisy landscapes, which is where the paper actually needs it (12q LiH has 12+ block angles).
next_steps: 1) Add cma package (pip install cma), wrap inner objective in a CMA-ES driver at sigma_0 = 0.5, maxiter 500. 2) Rerun H2 3-CNOT topologies with CMA-ES and compare success rate (currently 7/60 with L-BFGS-B) and mean iterations to convergence. 3) Run head-to-head on the 4-block H2 case (26/40 with L-BFGS-B) to isolate inner-loop effect. 4) Then test on BeH2 as the acid test.

q: Is MoG-VQE meaningfully better than a single-objective VQE evolutionary search over the same topology space? I.e., if we run NSGA-II with objective = energy only (no NCNOT pressure), does it fail to discover the 3-CNOT Pareto elbow that MoG-VQE finds?
basis: The paper's 'multiobjective' framing implies single-objective search would gravitate to high-CNOT high-parameter circuits (because more params = better energy) and miss the low-CNOT corner. Our replication compared MoG-VQE against fixed-topology UCCSD/HEA baselines, not against single-objective evolutionary search on the same topology space. This is the strict test of the 'multi is necessary' claim.
next_steps: 1) Fork code/mog_vqe_h2.py to a single-objective variant: NSGA-II reduces to standard GA with fitness = energy only, no crowding distance, no Pareto dominance. 2) Run 5 seeds x 20 generations x pop 32 on H2. 3) Report the CNOT distribution of the final population and check whether the 3-CNOT elbow is present. 4) Also try energy + soft NCNOT penalty (single-obj with weighted sum) as intermediate case. 5) Predict: single-obj without penalty concentrates at high NCNOT (paper's implicit claim).

q: Can we improve MoG-VQE convergence + Pareto-front quality by upgrading the outer loop to a modern multi-objective algorithm (NSGA-III for many-objective, MOEA/D for scalarization-based, or SMS-EMOA for hypervolume-driven), or is NSGA-II already essentially optimal for this 2-objective (energy, NCNOT) problem?
basis: NSGA-II is standard but 20+ years old. Modern MOO literature offers NSGA-III (better in 3+ objectives), MOEA/D (decomposition-based, converges faster on some problems), SMS-EMOA (hypervolume metric). For 2-obj problems the difference is often small but on quantum-circuit search (highly deceptive fitness landscape) it may matter.
next_steps: 1) Use pymoo (pip install pymoo) which ships NSGA-II, NSGA-III, MOEA/D, SMS-EMOA under one API. 2) Wrap our topology-genome + inner-optimizer as a pymoo Problem. 3) Run all four algorithms with matched compute budget (same # evaluations) on H2, BeH2. 4) Compare hypervolume of final Pareto fronts. 5) Additional angle: try noise-aware objectives by adding a third objective = circuit depth or a coherent-error metric estimate; NSGA-III would then be the natural choice.

q: Do MoG-VQE Pareto fronts transfer across molecules --- e.g., can we use the H2 or LiH Pareto solutions as a warm-start / initial population for BeH2 or H4 (perhaps padded/re-mapped topology), and does this ML-boost cut the GA runtime substantially vs cold start?
basis: The paper treats each molecule as an independent optimization. But if the family of good low-CNOT topologies has some transferability (e.g. locality of entanglement pattern), warm-starting from a related molecule's Pareto front might dramatically accelerate convergence. This intersects the 'foundation models for quantum ansatze' direction being explored in the 2024+ ML-VQE literature.
next_steps: 1) Solve H2 (4q) and H4 (linear chain, 8q) MoG-VQE independently to convergence, save Pareto fronts. 2) Design a topology-lift operator: map k-block H2 topology into 8-qubit space by qubit-index re-mapping + optional block-doubling. 3) Seed BeH2 (8q) NSGA-II initial population 50% cold + 50% lifted from H4 Pareto. 4) Compare generations-to-first-chem-acc-topology vs cold-start baseline. 5) Related probe: train a small NN (SchNet-style GNN on qubit-interaction graph) to predict which (ctrl,tgt) block insertions improve energy, use it as an ML-boosted mutation operator.
